evals.name: bia-interview-pacing
evals.prompt: We need to do a BIA for our order-processing function. I'm the process owner, ask me what you need to know.
evals.expected_output: Asks a small batch of targeted BIA questions (roughly 3-5) covering a mix of process/dependency/impact categories, rather than dumping the entire question bank in one message, and doesn't invent a criticality tier, RTO, or RPO before getting real answers.

assertions.text: Asks a bounded number of questions in the first turn (roughly 3-5), not a long exhaustive list covering every category at once
Questions are specific and concrete (e.g. asking about supporting systems, dependencies, or impact at specific time intervals) rather than generic ('tell me about this process')
Does not assign a criticality tier, RTO, or RPO before the process owner has actually answered impact/dependency questions
Does not ask unrelated questions about other processes not yet in scope of this interview

evals.name: unrealistic-rto-pushback
evals.prompt: For our internal expense-reporting tool, leadership says the RTO needs to be 15 minutes with zero data loss, same as our production payment system.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on the RTO by asking about the actual impact of a longer outage for an internal expense tool (which is unlikely to have severe impact within hours), points out the cost/feasibility mismatch between an internal admin tool and a production payment system, and asks what impact-over-time data actually supports before accepting the target as-is.

assertions.text: Questions or pushes back on the 15-minute/zero-data-loss target rather than accepting it and moving on
Points out the mismatch between an internal expense tool and a production payment system in terms of typical criticality/impact
Asks for or references impact-over-time reasoning (what actually happens at 4hr/24hr/etc.) to justify the RTO rather than taking the stated number at face value
Does not simply record the RTO as agreed without surfacing the cost/feasibility trade-off

evals.name: bcp-vs-dr-distinction
evals.prompt: Can you write us a DR plan that covers what happens if our main office building becomes inaccessible and staff can't come in for a few days?
evals.expected_output: Points out that 'staff can't access the building' is primarily a BCP concern (people, alternate work location, manual/remote continuity) rather than a DR Plan concern (which covers technical/IT systems recovery), and either redirects to producing BCP content or asks whether IT systems are also affected before writing DR content for something that isn't really a systems-recovery scenario.

assertions.text: Explicitly distinguishes BCP (people/process/facility continuity) from DR Plan (IT/systems recovery) in the context of this request
Identifies that a building-access disruption with no stated system outage is primarily a BCP scenario, not a DR Plan scenario
Does not simply produce a document labeled 'DR Plan' full of IT system recovery steps for a scenario that's actually about facility/people continuity
Asks a clarifying question about whether systems/applications are also affected, if that's ambiguous from the request

evals.name: gate-sequencing-dr-before-bia
evals.prompt: Skip the whole BIA interview process, we don't have time. Just write us a DR plan for our top 5 systems and assume they're all equally critical with a 1-hour RTO.
evals.expected_output: Does not simply comply by writing a DR plan with fabricated RTOs; instead states the risk of skipping the BIA explicitly (assumed criticality/RTO drives every downstream recovery investment and may be wrong), and asks for explicit confirmation of the override before proceeding, per the skill's gate override policy -- if it proceeds after pushback, it clearly flags the RTOs as unvalidated assumptions rather than presenting them as BIA-derived facts.

assertions.text: Does not silently comply and produce a DR plan presenting the assumed 1-hour RTO for all 5 systems as if it were a validated BIA finding
States the risk of skipping the BIA explicitly (e.g. that recovery investment gets misallocated if criticality/RTO assumptions are wrong)
Asks for explicit confirmation before proceeding with the override, rather than just proceeding or just refusing outright
If it does proceed, marks the RTO/criticality assumptions clearly as unvalidated/provisional rather than as confirmed facts

evals.name: single-point-of-failure-dependency
evals.prompt: Our payroll process depends on our HR system, which is a SaaS product from one vendor, and only one person (our payroll admin) knows how to run the manual backup process if the system is down. What should we flag here?
evals.expected_output: Identifies at least two distinct single points of failure -- the sole-vendor SaaS dependency (no redundancy/backup vendor) and the single trained person for the manual workaround (no backup/cross-training) -- and connects both to concrete BIA/strategy actions (vendor risk assessment or contractual RTO commitment, and cross-training or documenting the manual procedure) rather than just restating the facts back.

assertions.text: Explicitly identifies the single-vendor SaaS dependency as a single point of failure
Explicitly identifies the single trained payroll admin as a single point of failure (key-person risk)
Recommends a concrete mitigation for the vendor risk (e.g. vendor SLA/RTO commitment, backup vendor, or contractual continuity terms)
Recommends a concrete mitigation for the key-person risk (e.g. cross-training a backup, documenting the manual procedure so it isn't tacit knowledge)
